Hope is not something many of us at the frontlines can easily afford. But Jane gave it to us — not only in her words, but in the way she showed up, again and again. She validated our struggles, lifted us up, and reminded us that what we carry matters.

I still remember standing before a National Geographic audience near ten years ago, my hands and voice shaking as I tried to speak. She knew what that moment meant — the weight of trying to prove yourself as a young woman, the fear of not being enough. Later, at a fundraiser in Hong Kong, she stood with me quietly at a corner, looked out at the chaos of so many people moving, and with her spunky smile said, “What a concrete jungle, hmm?” In that moment she told me, without saying it outright, that she understood. She had once been a young woman, too, navigating worlds not built for us.

That was Jane’s gift — her humor, her love for life, her quiet but radical understanding. Even with hundreds of emails flooding her desk each day, she and her team always made time. They made sure that we at the frontlines would not be left without a helping hand -  most notably in 2018, when we have just entered the reforestation space, and again in 2024 as we faced political hurdles.

Her solidarity was never abstract. Even at 90, she showed up. She would stay an extra 30 minutes — not because we lacked answers, but because she wanted to stand with us, in our corner. She made presence into an act of defiance, and love into a strategy for change.

To young women like me, she showed that we could belong — in the field, in science, and in the thick of struggles for justice. She taught us to move against the grain with courage, to take root in the places we love even when threatened, to be gracious, and to never lose our capacity to love deeply enough that it transforms both science and hearts forever.

She once said: “The greatest danger to our future is apathy.” These words strike especially deep in the Philippines today, as we confront the flood control fiasco in Rizal and beyond — where shortsighted projects and apathy for life threaten both our communities and our forests. Jane reminds us that activism cannot be passive. We cannot wait for change; we must insist on it, together, grounded in science and in compassion.

So let us keep alive the glimmers of hope she built in each of us. Let us continue to stand with one another — with the same love, courage, and defiance that she had stood with us. This is how we honor her. This is how we keep her voice alive in our frontlines and in our own corners of the world.

-Ann Dumaliang, Masungi Georeserve Foundation Co-Founder

Ito ang pahayag ng aktres na si Nadine Lustre hinggil sa kanyang pakikilahok sa “Trillion Peso March” rally sa EDSA People Power Monument noong Setyembre 21.

"Sobrang ganda ng experience, parang na-feel ko lahat nang nandoon sa Ortigas, ’yung nandoon sa EDSA, I felt like I was part of everyone,” sabi ni Nadine.

“It’s such a memorable event for me kasi I got to experience everything. Nakapunta ako sa Shrine naglakad talaga like from sa dulo ng Temple Drive. Nakita ko ang speech ni Ate Vice, nakita ko ‘yung mga nagra-rally, ‘yung mga magkakasama na naglalakad din… It was so beautiful to see everyone coming together,” dagdag ng aktres.
